p.src: Now Zhou Yu stood atop the hill and watched for a long while. Suddenly he fell backward, vomited blood, and lost consciousness. His attendants carried him back to his tent. All the officers came to inquire after him. Utterly alarmed, they looked at one another and said, “North of the river stands an army of a million, crouching like a tiger and poised to swallow us like a whale. Who could have expected the Commander-in-Chief to be stricken thus? If Cao Cao’s troops arrive, what are we to do?” In haste they sent a report to the Marquis of Wu while summoning physicians to treat him.

p.src: When Lu Su saw Zhou Yu confined to bed by illness, he grew deeply troubled. He went to see Kongming and told him of Zhou Yu’s sudden collapse. Kongming asked, “What do you make of it?” Lu Su replied, “It is Cao Cao’s good fortune and Jiangdong’s calamity.” Kongming laughed. “I, Liang, can cure Gongjin’s illness.” Lu Su said, “If that is truly so, it would be the greatest blessing for our state!” He immediately invited Kongming to accompany him and examine the patient. Lu Su entered first to see Zhou Yu. Zhou Yu lay with the quilt pulled over his head. Lu Su asked, “How grave is your illness, Commander-in-Chief?” Zhou Yu replied, “My chest and belly are wracked with pain, and from time to time I lose consciousness.” Lu Su asked, “What medicines have you taken?” Zhou Yu said, “My stomach rebels with nausea, and I cannot keep the medicine down.” Lu Su said, “I have just been to see Kongming, who says he can cure your illness. He is outside the tent now. Shall I ask him to come and treat you?”

p.src: Zhou Yu ordered that he be admitted, then had his attendants help him sit up on the bed. Kongming said, “I have not seen you for several days. Who would have thought that you had fallen ill?” Zhou Yu said, “‘Fortune and calamity may befall a man between dawn and dusk.’ How can anyone secure himself against them?” Kongming laughed. “‘Heaven has winds and clouds no man can foresee.’ How, indeed, could anyone predict them?” At these words Zhou Yu’s face changed, and he began to groan. Kongming asked, “Do you feel some pent-up vexation within, Commander-in-Chief?” Zhou Yu replied, “I do.” Kongming said, “Then cooling medicine must be used to dispel it.” Zhou Yu said, “I have already taken cooling medicine, but it had no effect whatever.” Kongming said, “First your vital breath must be put in order; once it flows smoothly, every breath will naturally bring recovery.”

p.src: Zhou Yu guessed that Kongming must know what was on his mind, and tested him by asking, “What medicine should I take to make my vital breath flow smoothly?” Kongming laughed. “I have a prescription that will set your breath flowing smoothly at once.” Zhou Yu said, “Pray instruct me, Master.” Kongming called for brush and paper, dismissed all attendants, and secretly wrote sixteen characters: “To defeat Lord Cao, attack with fire; all is prepared—only the east wind is lacking.” When he had finished, he handed it to Zhou Yu and said, “This is the source of your illness, Commander-in-Chief.”

p.src: Zhou Yu was greatly startled when he read it and thought, “Kongming is truly more than mortal! He knew my thoughts all along! I have no choice but to tell him the truth.” Then he smiled and said, “Since you already know the source of my illness, Master, what medicine will you use to cure it? The situation is desperate; pray instruct me without delay.” Kongming said, “Though I, Liang, possess little talent, I once met an extraordinary man who transmitted to me the celestial books of the wondrous arts of Qimen Dunjia, by which I can summon wind and call down rain. If you require a southeast wind, have an altar built on Mount Nanping and call it the Altar of the Seven Stars. It must be nine feet high and built in three tiers, with one hundred and twenty men surrounding it, banners in hand. I shall perform the rites atop it and borrow a mighty southeast wind for three days and three nights to aid your operations. What say you?” Zhou Yu said, “Never mind three days and three nights. One night of strong wind would suffice to accomplish our great design. But the matter is immediately before us and admits no delay.” Kongming said, “What if I conduct the wind sacrifice on the twentieth day of the eleventh month, the jiazi day, and the wind ceases on the twenty-second, the bingyin day?”

p.src: Kongming took his leave and emerged from the tent. He and Lu Su mounted their horses and went to Mount Nanping to survey the terrain, where he ordered the soldiers to build the altar with red earth taken from the southeast. It measured twenty-four zhang across; each tier was three feet high, making nine feet in all. On the lowest tier were planted the banners of the Twenty-Eight Mansions: seven blue banners in the east, corresponding to Horn, Neck, Root, Room, Heart, Tail, and Winnowing Basket, arranged in the form of the Azure Dragon; seven black banners in the north, corresponding to Dipper, Ox, Girl, Emptiness, Rooftop, Encampment, and Wall, arrayed in the posture of the Black Tortoise; seven white banners in the west, corresponding to Legs, Bond, Stomach, Hairy Head, Net, Turtle Beak, and Three Stars, displaying the might of the White Tiger; and seven red banners in the south, corresponding to Well, Ghost, Willow, Star, Extended Net, Wings, and Chariot, forming the likeness of the Vermilion Bird. Around the second tier stood sixty-four yellow banners, corresponding to the sixty-four hexagrams and divided among the eight positions. On the upper tier stood four men, each wearing a cap over bound hair, a black gauze robe, a phoenix-patterned vestment with a broad sash, red shoes, and a square-hemmed garment. At the front left stood one holding a long pole topped with a plume of chicken feathers to catch the first sign of wind; at the front right stood one holding a long pole from which hung a Seven Stars pennant to reveal the character of the wind; at the rear left stood one bearing a precious sword; and at the rear right stood one bearing an incense burner. Below the altar, twenty-four men encircled all four sides, each holding such objects as standards, ceremonial canopies, great halberds, long spears, yellow yak-tail standards, white battle-axes, red banners, and black streamers.

p.src: At the auspicious hour on the jiazi day, the twentieth of the eleventh month, Kongming bathed, fasted, and purified himself. Wearing Daoist robes, barefoot and with his hair unbound, he came before the altar and instructed Lu Su: “Zijing, return to the army and help Gongjin deploy the troops. If my prayer brings no response, do not hold it against me.” Lu Su took his leave and departed. Kongming charged the officers and soldiers guarding the altar: “None may leave his assigned position without permission. None may put heads together and whisper. None may let slip any wild words. None may raise an alarm or make a commotion. Whoever disobeys shall be beheaded!” All received the command. Kongming slowly ascended the altar. Having inspected the fixed positions, he burned incense in the burner, poured water into a bowl, raised his face to heaven, and prayed in silence. He descended and entered the tent to rest awhile, ordering the soldiers to take turns eating. Kongming ascended the altar three times and descended three times that day, yet no southeast wind appeared.

p.src: Meanwhile, Zhou Yu had Cheng Pu, Lu Su, and the other officers wait in his tent. They had only to await the rising of the southeast wind before deploying the troops; at the same time, he sent word to Sun Quan to be ready to support them. Huang Gai had already prepared twenty fire ships. Their bows were densely studded with large nails, while their holds were packed with reeds and dry firewood soaked in fish oil and topped with sulfur, saltpeter, and other combustibles. Each load was concealed beneath an oiled blue-cloth cover. Green dragon-tooth banners were planted at the bows, and a swift skiff was tied to the stern of each ship. Huang Gai waited below the command tent for Zhou Yu’s order. Gan Ning and Kan Ze kept Cai He and Cai Zhong confined within the naval stockade. They drank wine every day and allowed not a single soldier to go ashore. Eastern Wu’s troops surrounded them on every side, sealing the place so tightly that not even water could escape. They too awaited only the order from headquarters.

p.src: As Zhou Yu sat deliberating in his tent, a scout came to report: “The Marquis of Wu’s ships lie at anchor eighty-five li from the stockade, awaiting only good news from you, Commander-in-Chief.” Zhou Yu immediately sent Lu Su to notify the officers and soldiers of every division: “Each of you must ready your ships, weapons, sails, oars, and all other equipment. Once the order is issued, do not delay for so much as a moment. If anyone errs or causes delay, military law shall be enforced.” The officers and men received the order. Each rubbed his fists and palms, readying himself for battle.

p.src: That day, as night drew near, the sky was clear and not a breath of wind stirred. Zhou Yu said to Lu Su, “Kongming's words were mistaken. How could a southeast wind arise in the depths of winter?” Lu Su replied, “I believe Kongming would never speak without good reason.” Near the third watch, the sound of wind was suddenly heard and the banners began to turn. When Zhou Yu went out of his tent to look, the banner tails were streaming toward the northwest; in an instant a strong southeast wind arose. Zhou Yu cried in horror, “This man possesses arts that wrest the workings of creation from Heaven and Earth, and mysteries unfathomable even to ghosts and gods! If he is allowed to live, he will become the root of disaster for the Southland. We must kill him at once and forestall future trouble.” He hastily summoned Ding Feng and Xu Sheng, the two commandants of his guard, and ordered, “Take one hundred men apiece. Xu Sheng shall go by river and Ding Feng by land; both of you are to reach the Seven-Star Altar on Mount Nanping. Ask no questions: seize Zhuge Liang, behead him at once, and bring me his head to claim your reward.” The two generals received their orders. Xu Sheng boarded a vessel, and his hundred axemen thrust out their oars and set off; Ding Feng mounted his horse, and his hundred crossbowmen each bestrode a charger and rode toward Mount Nanping. On the way, they met the southeast wind rising full against them. A later poet wrote:

p.src: Ding Feng's cavalry arrived first and saw the soldiers bearing banners upon the altar, standing in the wind. Ding Feng dismounted, climbed the altar with sword in hand, and, finding Kongming gone, anxiously questioned its guards. They replied, “He left the altar just moments ago.” Ding Feng hurried down to search for him, just as Xu Sheng's ship arrived. The two met at the riverbank. p.src: Xu Sheng saw that the boat ahead had no sail and pressed on heedlessly. When they had nearly closed the distance, Zhao Yun nocked an arrow, drew his bow, and shouted from the stern, “I am Zhao Zilong of Changshan! I have come by command expressly to receive the Military Adviser. Why do you pursue him? I would have shot you dead with a single arrow, but that would damage the amity between our two houses. So I shall merely show you what I can do!” As he finished speaking, his arrow flew and severed the sail rope on Xu Sheng's vessel. The sail fell into the water, and the vessel swung broadside. Zhao Yun then had his own boat's sail raised to its full spread and sped away before the following wind. His boat flew like an arrow, and pursuit was impossible.

p.src: Zhou Yu accepted his advice and summoned all his generals to receive their orders. First he ordered Gan Ning, “Take Cai Zhong and the surrendered soldiers along the south bank. Display only the banners of the northern army and make straight for Wulin, where Cao Cao's grain stores are situated. Penetrate deep into the army and raise fires as your signal. Leave Cai He alone here under my command; I have a use for him.” Second he summoned Taishi Ci and instructed him, “Lead three thousand soldiers straight to the borders of Huangzhou, cut off Cao Cao's reinforcements from Hefei, then press close upon Cao's army and light fires as your signal. When you see red banners, that will mean the Marquis of Wu's reinforcing troops have arrived.” These two forces, having the farthest to go, departed first. Third, he ordered Lü Meng to lead three thousand soldiers to Wulin in support of Gan Ning when he set Cao Cao's camp and stockades ablaze. Fourth, he ordered Ling Tong to lead three thousand soldiers directly to the border of Yiling and, upon seeing fires rise at Wulin, bring his troops into action in support. Fifth, he ordered Dong Xi to lead three thousand soldiers straight to Hanyang, charge from Hanchuan into Cao Cao's camp, and watch for white banners signaling support. Sixth, he ordered Pan Zhang to lead three thousand soldiers, all bearing white banners, to Hanyang in support of Dong Xi.

Zhou Yu then ordered Huang Gai to prepare the fire ships and sent a soldier galloping away with a letter arranging his surrender to Cao Cao that night. At the same time, four warships were assigned to follow behind Huang Gai's vessels in support. Han Dang commanded the first division, Zhou Tai the second, Jiang Qin the third, and Chen Wu the fourth. Each division led three hundred warships, with twenty fire ships arrayed at its head. Zhou Yu and Cheng Pu personally directed the battle from a great tower ship, with Xu Sheng and Ding Feng guarding them on either side. p.src: Meanwhile, Sun Quan sent an envoy bearing a military tally, with word that Lu Xun had been appointed vanguard and ordered to advance directly into the Qi and Huang regions, while the Marquis of Wu himself would support him from the rear. Zhou Yu also sent men to fire signal cannon on the Western Hills and raise signal flags on Mount Nanping. When every preparation was complete, they waited only for dusk to make their move.

p.src: Now the tale divides. Liu Xuande was at Xiakou, anxiously awaiting Kongming's return, when he suddenly saw a fleet approach. It was Young Lord Liu Qi, who had come in person to learn the news. Xuande invited him up to the watchtower, and when they were seated said, “The southeast wind has been blowing for some time. Zilong went to meet Kongming, yet neither has returned, and I am deeply troubled.” A junior officer pointed toward the harbor at Fankou and said, “A single sail is bringing a light boat before the wind. It must be the Military Adviser.” Xuande and Liu Qi descended the tower to welcome him. Presently the boat arrived, and Kongming and Zilong came ashore. Xuande was overjoyed. When greetings were over, Kongming said, “There is no time now to speak of anything else. Are the soldiers and warships we arranged earlier all ready?” Xuande replied, “They have long been prepared and await only your orders, Military Adviser.”

p.src: Kongming entered the command tent with Xuande and Liu Qi and, when they were seated, said to Zhao Yun, “Zilong, take three thousand troops across the river, proceed by the narrow road to Wulin, and lie in ambush where the trees and reeds grow thick. After the fourth watch tonight, Cao Cao is certain to flee along that road. Let his troops pass, then set fires in the midst of them. Even if you cannot annihilate them, you will destroy half.” Zhao Yun said, “There are two roads from Wulin: one leads to Nanjun and the other to Jingzhou. Which road will he take?” Kongming replied, “Nanjun is too closely pressed, so Cao Cao will not dare go there. He will certainly come by way of Jingzhou, and then lead his main army on toward Xuchang.”

p.src: Zhao Yun received the plan and departed. Kongming then summoned Zhang Fei and said, “Yide, lead three thousand soldiers across the river, cut off the road through Yiling, and lie in ambush at the mouth of Calabash Valley. Cao Cao will not dare take the road through Southern Yiling but will certainly head toward Northern Yiling. Tomorrow, after the rain, his men will surely halt to set up their cooking pots and prepare a meal. As soon as you see smoke rise, set fire along the mountainside. Even if you fail to capture Cao Cao, your achievement in this battle will surely be considerable.”

p.src: Zhang Fei received his instructions and departed. Then he summoned Mi Zhu, Mi Fang, and Liu Feng, ordering each of them to command a flotilla. They were to scour the river, capture the routed troops, and seize their weapons and equipment. The three received their instructions and departed. Kongming rose and said to the young lord Liu Qi, “Wuchang, which lies within sight of here, is a place of the utmost importance. You should return there at once. Lead your troops and array them at the river landing. Once Cao Cao is defeated, fugitives will surely come that way; seize them as they arrive, but on no account venture far from the city.” Liu Qi took leave of Xuande and Kongming and departed. Kongming said to Xuande, “My lord, you may station your troops at Fankou, look down from the heights, and sit at ease while Zhou Yu accomplishes a great victory tonight.”

p.src: Guan Yu was standing nearby, but Kongming paid him no attention whatsoever. Unable to contain himself, Guan Yu called out loudly, “Ever since I began following my elder brother on his campaigns many years ago, I have never once held back. Now that we face a mighty enemy, why does the military adviser give me no assignment?” Kongming laughed. “Do not take offense, Guan Yu! I had intended to trouble you with guarding the most vital of all the passes, but unfortunately there is a certain obstacle, so I dare not send you.” Guan Yu asked, “What obstacle is there? Tell me at once.” Kongming said, “In former days Cao Cao treated you with great generosity, and you must feel some obligation to repay him. When Cao Cao is defeated today, he will certainly flee by the Huarong Road. If I send you there, you are certain to let him pass. That is why I dare not send you.”

p.src: Guan Yu said, “You are far too suspicious, Master Strategist! Cao Cao did indeed treat me well in those days, but I repaid him by slaying Yan Liang and Wen Chou and lifting the siege of Baima. If I encounter him today, how could I possibly let him go lightly?” Kongming asked, “And what if you do let him go?” Guan Yu replied, “I will submit to military law.” Kongming said, “Then put it in writing.” Guan Yu accordingly gave him a written military pledge. Then Guan Yu asked, “What if Cao Cao does not come by that road?” Kongming replied, “Then I too will give you a written military pledge.” Guan Yu was delighted. Kongming said, “At a high place beside the narrow Huarong track, pile up brushwood and set it alight so that the smoke will draw Cao Cao toward you.” Guan Yu said, “If Cao Cao sees the smoke, he will know there is an ambush. Why would he come?” Kongming laughed. “Have you not heard the principle in the art of war by which emptiness is made to seem substantial and substance empty? Though Cao Cao is skilled in warfare, this alone will suffice to deceive him. When he sees the smoke, he will take it for an empty show and will certainly choose that road. General, you must show him no mercy.”

p.src: Guan Yu received his orders and led Guan Ping, Zhou Cang, and five hundred broadsword-bearing troops away to lie in ambush on the Huarong Road. Xuande said, “My brother’s sense of honor runs deep. If Cao Cao truly takes the Huarong Road, I fear he really will let him go.” Kongming replied, “Last night I observed the signs of heaven. The villain Cao is not yet fated to die. It will also be a fine thing to let Guan Yu perform this favor for him.” Xuande said, “Your divine foresight, Master, is rarely equaled in this world!” Kongming then went with Xuande to Fankou to observe Zhou Yu’s deployment, leaving Sun Qian and Jian Yong to guard the city.

p.src: Meanwhile, in his main camp, Cao Cao was conferring with his generals while awaiting news from Huang Gai. That day the southeast wind blew fiercely. Cheng Yu entered and warned Cao Cao, “A southeast wind has risen today. We should take precautions.” Cao Cao laughed. “At the winter solstice the yang force is born anew; when its cycle returns, how could there fail to be a southeast wind? What is there to wonder at?” A soldier suddenly reported that a small boat had arrived from the eastern bank bearing a secret letter from Huang Gai. Cao Cao ordered the messenger brought in at once, and the man presented the letter. The letter said, “Zhou Yu’s security is so strict that I have found no means of escape. Now grain newly transported from Poyang Lake has arrived, and Zhou Yu has assigned me to patrol it, giving me my opportunity. At all costs I shall kill one of Jiangdong’s renowned generals and bring his head when I surrender. At the third watch tonight, the vessels flying blue dragon swallowtail banners will be the grain ships.” Cao Cao was overjoyed. He went with his generals to a great ship in the naval stockade and watched for Huang Gai’s arrival.

p.src: Meanwhile in Jiangdong, as evening drew on, Zhou Yu had Cai He brought forth and ordered the soldiers to bind him and throw him down. Cai He cried, “I am innocent!” Zhou Yu said, “What sort of man are you, to dare come here feigning surrender? I happen to lack a sacrificial offering for the banners, so I should like to borrow your head.” Unable to deny it any longer, Cai He shouted, “Your own Kan Ze and Gan Ning were party to the plot as well!” Zhou Yu replied, “They were acting on my orders.” Cai He’s regrets came too late. Zhou Yu had him dragged to the riverbank beneath the black command banner. Wine was poured and ritual paper burned; then Cai He was beheaded with a single stroke. When the banner had been consecrated with his blood, Zhou Yu ordered the fleet to set sail. Huang Gai stood aboard the third fire ship, wearing only a breastplate and gripping a keen blade. Upon his banner were written in large characters: “Vanguard Huang Gai.” Taking advantage of the fair wind, Huang Gai advanced toward Red Cliffs.

p.src: By then the east wind was blowing with tremendous force, and the waves surged high. From the center of his formation, Cao Cao gazed across the river. The rising moon shone upon the water, where the rippling waves seemed like ten thousand golden serpents at play. Facing the wind, Cao Cao laughed aloud, believing his triumph assured. Suddenly a soldier pointed and said, “A cluster of sails can be faintly seen to the south, coming before the wind.” Cao Cao looked down from his vantage point, and a man reported, “They are all flying blue dragon swallowtail banners. Among them is a great banner bearing the name ‘Vanguard Huang Gai.’” Cao Cao laughed. “Huang Gongfu comes to surrender. Heaven itself is aiding me!”

p.src: The approaching ships drew nearer. After observing them for a long while, Cheng Yu said to Cao Cao, “Those ships must be part of a deception. Do not allow them near the stockade yet.” Cao Cao asked, “How do you know?” Cheng Yu replied, “A ship laden with grain must ride low and steady. But the ships before us sit high and light upon the water. Moreover, tonight’s southeast wind is exceedingly strong. If this is a stratagem, how shall we withstand it?” Cao Cao realized the danger and asked at once, “Who will go and stop them?” Wen Ping said, “I am well acquainted with fighting on the water. Allow me to go.” With that, he leaped into a small boat. At a signal from his hand, more than ten patrol boats followed him out. Standing in the bow, Wen Ping shouted, “By the prime minister’s august command, the southern ships are not to approach the stockade. Cast anchor in midstream!” His men shouted in unison, “Lower your sails at once!”

p.src: Before the words had left their mouths, a bowstring twanged. An arrow struck Wen Ping in the left arm, and he fell into the boat. His flotilla fell into confusion, and the boats fled back separately. The southern ships were now only two li of water away from Cao Cao’s stockade. Huang Gai signaled with his sword, and all the ships in the van burst into flame. The fire rode the force of the wind and the wind swelled the fury of the flames. The ships flew like arrows, while smoke and fire blotted out the sky. Twenty fire ships smashed into the naval stockade. In an instant, every ship in Cao Cao’s stockade was ablaze. Bound together with iron rings, they had no means of escape. Cannon fire sounded from across the river, and fire ships closed in from every side. Over the whole expanse of the Three Rivers, flames raced with the wind; all was a single crimson blaze stretching from earth to heaven.

p.src: Cao Cao looked back toward the camps on shore and saw smoke and fire rising in several places. Huang Gai leaped into a small boat, which several men rowed from behind, and pushed through smoke and flame in search of Cao Cao. Seeing the danger, Cao Cao was just about to leap ashore when Zhang Liao arrived in a light skiff. By the time he had helped Cao Cao down into it, the great ship was already burning. Zhang Liao and a dozen men guarded Cao Cao as they sped toward the landing. Huang Gai saw a man in a crimson robe descend into a boat and guessed that it was Cao Cao. Urging his boat swiftly forward, he raised his keen blade and shouted, “Villain Cao, do not flee! Huang Gai is here!” Cao Cao cried out repeatedly in dismay. Zhang Liao took up his bow and nocked an arrow. Waiting until Huang Gai had drawn near, he loosed it at him. The wind was roaring at its height, and amid the glare of the flames, how could Huang Gai hear the bowstring sing? The arrow struck him squarely in the shoulder, and he toppled backward into the water. Indeed:
